subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which scientist provided evidence for the existence of the neutron?
questions.explain: James Chadwick's experiments (about 20 years after the nuclear model) provided evidence for the neutron. Bohr proposed electron energy levels; Thomson devised the plum pudding model.

questions.q: What was Bohr's key contribution to the development of the atomic model?
options: He suggested electrons orbit the nucleus at specific fixed distances (energy levels)
He fired alpha particles at gold foil
He proposed the plum pudding model
questions.explain: Bohr adapted the nuclear model by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances (energy levels), which matched experimental observations.

questions.q: For an object (such as the Earth) to stay at a constant temperature, what must be true about its radiation?
options: It neither absorbs nor emits radiation
It absorbs more radiation than it emits
The rate it absorbs radiation equals the rate it emits radiation
It emits more radiation than it absorbs
questions.explain: Temperature stays constant when the power absorbed equals the power emitted. If absorption exceeds emission the object warms; if emission exceeds absorption it cools.

questions.q: Heating a substance without changing its state increases its internal energy. Specifically, it increases the particles'...
options: kinetic energy, so the temperature rises
potential energy only, so temperature stays constant
questions.explain: When heating raises temperature (no state change), the energy increases the particles' kinetic energy, so they move faster and the temperature rises.

questions.q: Work is done on an object when a force makes it move. What energy transfer often warms the surroundings when work is done against friction?
options: Energy is destroyed by the friction
Energy is transferred to the thermal store, raising temperature
questions.explain: Work done against friction transfers energy to the thermal store of the object and surroundings, so they warm up. Energy is conserved, not created or destroyed.

questions.q: Which particles are found inside the nucleus of an atom?
questions.explain: The nucleus contains protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral). Electrons (negative) orbit the nucleus in energy levels (shells).

questions.q: What will happen to the Sun (a low-mass star) when it runs low on hydrogen fuel?
options: It will expand into a red giant, then become a white dwarf
It will explode as a supernova
It will become a neutron star
It will become a black hole
questions.explain: A low-mass star like the Sun swells into a red giant, then sheds its outer layers and the core becomes a white dwarf that slowly cools.

questions.q: Which of these quantities is a scalar?
questions.explain: A scalar has magnitude only. Distance is a scalar; force, displacement and acceleration all have direction, so they are vectors. (Distance vs displacement is a common trap.)

questions.q: In the required practical, how can you measure the speed of waves in a ripple tank?
options: Time how long the tank takes to fill
Measure only the depth of water
Measure the amplitude and double it
Measure the frequency and wavelength, then use v = fλ
questions.explain: You find the frequency (e.g. from the wave generator or by counting waves per second) and the wavelength (e.g. from a stroboscope or by measuring several waves), then calculate v = fλ.

questions.q: What is the specific latent heat of vaporisation of a substance?
options: The energy to melt 1 g of the substance
The energy to change the state of 1 kg from solid to liquid
The energy to raise 1 kg by 1°C
The energy to change the state of 1 kg from liquid to gas with no temperature change
questions.explain: Specific latent heat of vaporisation is the energy needed to change 1 kg of a substance from liquid to gas (or back) at constant temperature. Latent heat of fusion refers to the solid↔liquid change.

questions.q: Why does light bend (refract) when it passes from air into glass?
options: It speeds up in the glass
Its speed changes, which changes its direction (unless it hits the boundary along the normal)
questions.explain: Refraction happens because the wave changes speed when it enters a different medium. Light slows down in glass; if it meets the boundary at an angle, this change of speed bends it toward the normal.

questions.q: What is meant by the internal energy of a system?
options: The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles
Only the kinetic energy of the particles
The energy supplied by an external heater
Only the potential energy stored between particles
questions.explain: Internal energy is the total energy stored by the particles: the sum of their kinetic energy (from motion) and the potential energy stored in the bonds/forces between them.

questions.q: What happens when an electron in an atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation of the right energy?
options: It leaves the atom and becomes a neutron
It moves to a lower energy level
It moves to a higher energy level (further from the nucleus)
questions.explain: Absorbing EM radiation can move an electron to a higher energy level. When it falls back to a lower level it emits EM radiation.

questions.q: What is nuclear fusion?
options: A large unstable nucleus splitting into two smaller nuclei
Two light nuclei joining to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
A nucleus emitting an alpha particle
questions.explain: Fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy (as in the Sun). Fission is the splitting of a large unstable nucleus into smaller ones.

questions.q: Which energy resource is most reliable for continuous large-scale electricity generation?
questions.explain: Fossil-fuel power stations can run on demand at any time, making them reliable, whereas solar, wind and wave depend on the weather and time of day.

questions.q: Which of these is the correct SI base unit of mass?
questions.explain: The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram (kg). The gram is a smaller unit, the newton is the unit of force, and the pound is not an SI unit.

questions.q: Hooke's law states that, up to the limit of proportionality, the extension of a spring is:
options: Directly proportional to the force applied
questions.explain: Hooke's law: extension is directly proportional to the force, so F = ke. This holds only up to the limit of proportionality, beyond which the relationship is no longer linear.

questions.q: In what direction do magnetic field lines around a bar magnet point?
options: From north pole to south pole outside the magnet
From south pole to north pole outside the magnet
questions.explain: By convention, magnetic field lines travel from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet. The direction is the direction of the force on a north pole.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. The table pushes up on the book. Which is the Newton's third law pair to this force?
options: The weight of the book pulling down
The book pushing down on the table
The air pressure on the book
questions.explain: Newton's third law pairs are equal, opposite, act on different objects and are the same type of force (contact). The table pushing up on the book pairs with the book pushing down on the table.

questions.q: On a velocity–time graph, what does the area under the line represent?
questions.explain: The area under a velocity–time graph equals velocity × time, which gives the distance travelled. The gradient gives the acceleration.

questions.q: Which quantity is measured in a derived unit rather than an SI base unit?
questions.explain: A derived unit is built from base units. Speed (m/s) is metres divided by seconds, so it is derived. The second, metre and kilogram are SI base units.

questions.q: When ice melts to form water, what happens to the total mass?
questions.explain: Melting is a physical change: no particles are created or destroyed, so mass is conserved. The water has the same mass as the ice it came from.
